p: In February a tech sergeant named Rae Sutter told Kit, kindly and in front of the break room, that you have to be in pilot training before thirty three, so she was done. Kit thanked her and went to read the page herself.

At Vern's table the posting said her age is measured on the board date, July 10, which still left her five weeks over. Page two also set a minimum PCSM score, which means booking the TBAS, a separate computer test.

Vern had read the longer rule behind the posting, and it settled the rumor: age goes by the board date, and Sutter's version was the rule years ago. The long rule also has an exception to policy for someone just outside the line, and the unit has to sponsor it: the colonel's name, and then a yes or no from above the wing. Vern had known since January and waited for her to ask. Kit asked him what a request like that needs, not for a word with the colonel, and he said he doesn't call colonels.

At the water plant her supervisor, Gene Albers, told the morning huddle the state had cut their sampling to eight a month. A footnote said that only comes after a clean year and the state's okay in writing. Kit showed him in private, and he fixed it himself.

Graham laid out twelve weeks of study on the fridge whiteboard, gave her his Saturday mornings, and wrote May 15 in the corner. Her mother had heard the rumor secondhand, and Kit told her about the board herself.
Vern circled the words the wing seven times in her letter of intent and asked who it was from. That Saturday night Kit typed one new sentence, I want to fly, and couldn't make herself print it.
Two Tuesdays went by without the sentence, and Vern asked once.

On the first one he asked as she sat down, and she said not yet. He nodded and opened the reading book where they'd left off. On the second he let it be. At the end of the night he handed her a log out of the box, the way he always did, and she put it in her coat without reading it. LETTER 2 sat on the laptop next to LETTER, and she left them both shut.

Saturday, March 6, was drill. At ten to four in the morning the launch board in the shop had two two eight flying at eight thirty, and next to it, in Boyd's block printing, DARROW. The full timers had left a note on the board from Friday's postflight. One of the tires on the left main gear was worn to limits. It had to come off before the jet went anywhere.

Fisk came in at five after four with his ears red and the scanner lanyard still around his neck. Nine and a half hours at the distribution center, he said, when she asked. I'm good, Sergeant. She looked at him a second longer than she needed to, and then she let it go. He'd done four wheel changes with her since the fall, and one of Kemp's airmen was free to help. She gave him the wheel and went to start her walkaround.
Vern's Nav Table: integrity, and saying it straight.
I held a jet on the ground over my own arithmetic more than once. Nobody on the ramp ever thanked me for it. Nobody ever had to.

You've had the rule twice now, and its one exception. Here's how to tell when the exception applies. Ask three things. Is something false or unsafe? Is it about to be used, by a jet, a report, a commander, anyone who'll sign or act on it? And is it still moving, not already caught and fixed? If all three are yes, the most effective action usually stops it and tells the person who needs to know, right away.

That doesn't throw out the rest of the key. You still go to your own supervisor before the office above them. You still say it face to face, not on a channel the whole base hears. You can still give the person involved a private word first, as long as it doesn't hold up the stop or the report. What changes is the clock.

Notice what the most effective option in these items usually leaves out. It doesn't decide what happens to the person. That belongs to the chain above you. Your part is to stop it, report it, and tell the truth about your own share of it.
How the exam asks it. When an option quietly fixes the problem and tells nobody, look at it hard for least effective. A quiet fix leaves the false record in place, and the habit with it.

Integrity and Professionalism items tend to share a shape. Somebody did something wrong, maybe you, and one of the options makes it go away without anyone finding out. Signing for work you didn't see. Rounding a number up for a boss. Covering for a friend. Keeping a gift you shouldn't. That option is rarely the most effective, and it's often the least.

Your own mistakes count too. When the error is yours, owning the mistake is the effective move: report it yourself, early, to the person it affects, along with what you've already done about it. Waiting to see whether anybody notices is the low one.
A signature says you did the thing or saw it done. On the flight line and on this test, signing for work you didn't do or didn't see falsifies the record, even if the work turns out fine.

Loyalty doesn't change this. The key does reward taking care of your people. It doesn't reward a cover up that protects them from the record of what they did. Taking care of them is what happens after the record's straight.

Try one. You're a lieutenant. In the morning meeting you told your commander every fire extinguisher in the hangar had its monthly check. An hour later you learn the airman you gave it to never got to the back row. Nobody else knows. Getting them checked fast and saying nothing is low, because it makes your words true after the fact and leaves the commander trusting a report that wasn't. Hoping it never comes up is lower. The best pick goes back to the commander today, says what you told them was wrong, and says when the back row will be done. Being honest about your own miss feels worse than being honest about somebody else's. It's the same rule, and it's the integrity item people talk themselves out of.
How the exam asks it. If the problem is yours, look for the option where you report it before anybody asks.

Communication items are about who hears what, from whom, and when. Bad news goes early, and it comes from you. If you promised your people something and it fell through, tell them yourself, say why, and say what happens next. Letting them read it off a schedule is lower. Blaming the people above you is lower still.

When you're carrying out a decision you didn't make and don't like, explain it to your people the way it was explained to you, and take your disagreement up the chain in private. Running the decision down in front of your airmen is one of the lowest picks there is. It costs your commander their trust in you, and it costs you your airmen's trust in both of you.
If something changes another person's work, they should hear it from you directly. The secondhand version is the one with the qualifiers gone.

Communication runs up the chain too. If you made a call your supervisor is going to hear about, tell them first, yourself, with what you did and why. A boss who hears it from somebody else has to wonder what else they haven't heard.
How the exam asks it. When you disagree with an order, look for the option that carries it out and questions it in private.

The hardest pairs on this subtest are two options that say the same thing. One says it to the person, privately. The other says it in a huddle, on a radio, or in an email to the whole section. The content's right in both, and the audience decides it.

Timing works the same way. Telling your supervisor on Monday is fine in a normal week and wrong if the jet flies Saturday. Before you pick most effective, ask who hears it and when. Before you pick least, look for the option that does real harm: a false record kept, a person shamed in front of others, a supervisor skipped.
How the exam asks it. Two options with the same message? Prefer the one that reaches the right people soonest without an audience it doesn't need.

On test day the subtests come in one order, back to back. Verbal Analogies runs eight minutes and hands you straight to twenty nine minutes of word problems. Practice them that way at least once a week: a timed analogy block, then arithmetic, with no break between. The switch costs you a minute the first few times, and you'd rather spend that minute at a kitchen table than in a test center.
Before a practice sitting, write the order and the minutes down from the current Pearson page, and check what you wrote against the page. A practice run on the wrong clock teaches the wrong pace.
How the exam asks it. Read the first word problem after the analogies twice. Right after a fast subtest is an easy place for a careless miss.

Resource management items hand you more work than you have people, hours, money or equipment, and ask what you do about it. The key's top pick usually sorts the work first, before it starts on any of it. Safety goes first, and anything with a hard deadline from above. Then what only you can do. Then what you can delegate, and to whom. A tired airman counts as a resource too, and the plan has to count the hours they've already worked.

Say you're a lieutenant with three airmen, a shift that ends at six, and three jobs. A tool inventory is due to the inspector at noon. A truck has to be checked before it leaves at two. Your commander wants a briefing on Friday. The low pick works all three at once with everybody, or takes them in the order they showed up. The better one puts two airmen on the inventory and one on the truck, keeps the briefing for you after noon, and tells the commander Friday is safe. You prioritize by the clock and the risk, and you can say the plan in one breath.

Two traps. The first is the hero option, where you stay all night and do it yourself. It looks like dedication. The key usually ranks it low, because it wastes the people you have and wears out the one person who needs to be sharp tomorrow. I flew with a major once who tried to fly every hard sortie on the schedule himself, and by spring he was very tired and very wrong. The second trap is asking for more manpower before you've used what you've got. Ask, sure, after you can show the workload doesn't fit.
How the exam asks it. When an option has you doing everyone's work yourself, look at it for the low end. Sorting and handing out the work usually beats heroics.

Innovation items start with a better way. You, or one of your people, can see how a job could go faster, cheaper or safer. The key's top pick usually doesn't switch on the spot, and it doesn't sit on the idea either. It writes the idea down, takes it to whoever owns the process, and offers to try it small, where a failure costs little.

Here's one. An airman of yours has worked out a new approach to the launch lineup: text each crew its jet and times on Friday night, instead of everybody reading the board at six in the morning. You think it would buy every crew twenty minutes. The low pick is trying it quietly on your own crews without telling anyone. The lineup belongs to the scheduling office, and two versions of it on one morning is how a jet gets missed. Nearly as low is telling the airman to drop it in the yearly suggestion box. The better pick is helping them write it up and walking it to the scheduler, with the airman's name on it.

Watch for the option that's bold and skips the owner. It sounds like initiative, and the key tends to rank it below the slower one that goes through the right person. Watch, too, for the option that kills an idea because it's new. Propose a change, try it small, measure it, then spread it. The best change I ever saw on a crew started as a strip of tape on a captain's panel with three numbers on it. He took it to the standards shop before he showed anybody else, and two years later it was in the checklist.
How the exam asks it. A good idea put in place without the owner's okay usually ranks below the same idea brought to the owner first.

Mentoring items ask what you do with a person who could be doing better. The key's top pick is usually teaching them, not doing it for them and not writing them up first. Find out why the mistake keeps happening. Show them once, watch them do it, and check back.

Say a new airman signs a form in the wrong block for the second week running. Fixing it yourself every Friday is in the low middle. It keeps the form right and the airman wrong. Telling them off in front of the shop is lower. The better pick is ten minutes of coaching beside them with the form, then watching them fill out the next one and saying so when it's right. The man who taught me celestial made me shoot the same star nine nights running, and he never once took the sextant out of my hands.

Counseling is the formal side, and it has an order too. A written counseling usually follows the talk that didn't work, not the first mistake, unless that first mistake is serious. A safety or integrity breach can go straight to writing. And mentoring isn't only for people who are struggling. The key also tends to reward the officer who notices a sharp airman and points them at a course, a harder job or a board. Develop people before they ask. After a miss on the flight line, retraining isn't punishment. It's how the next signature comes to mean something.
How the exam asks it. Between fixing an airman's work for them and teaching them to do it, the key usually favors teaching.
Fisk and the airman had the jack under the gear and the first tool out at 4:40. Kit wrote the time on the back of a work card, the way she wrote down everything on a launch morning.

The shop's planning number for a main wheel was an hour and a half with two people. After that came her inspection, twenty minutes if she took her time, and she always took it. The crew bus was due at seven. She wanted the jet done, wheel and inspection both, before the bus doors opened.
How much slack is in her morning, at the shop's numbers?
A. Ten minutes, with the wheel at an hour fifty.
B. Thirty minutes, after the wheel and her inspection.
C. An hour and ten, seven less four forty less the work.
D. Fifty minutes, from the wheel being done to the bus.
Ninety minutes from 4:40 is 6:10. Her twenty makes it 6:30. Thirty minutes to the bus. She wrote 30 at the bottom of the card and circled it, and stopped thinking about it until it was gone.

That'll hold, Sergeant. Start, plus the job, plus the check, against the deadline. Ninety minutes is an hour thirty, so 6:10, then 6:30, then thirty minutes to seven. The wrong choices on this subtest are built out of the steps people skip. Did you count every one?

At 5:30 she came around the nose with her flashlight and found Fisk on his knees by the old tire, the bead finally broken loose. He was working the bar one slow pull at a time. Twice she watched him stop with his eyes shut and start again, and the second time she opened her mouth and then went on with her walkaround. The wind had swung around in the night. Out at midfield the windsock stood straight out the other way from Friday, and the tower had turned the runway around to match it.

Fisk sat back on his heels and looked out at the sock for a while before he said anything. They're going out the long way. Why not let the wind push them? He asked it the way you'd ask somebody the time.
A. Tell him a headwind gets the wings to flying speed in less runway.
B. Tell him a tailwind adds to the speed, and either way works.
C. Tell him the tower picks the end that's quieter for the town.
D. Tell him it's for stopping, if they have to abort the takeoff.

Wind in her face is free airspeed. She held her glove up into it, flat, and the river wind about took it off her hand. Fifteen knots of that and she's got fifteen knots over the wings parked at the hold line. Turn her around and she has to buy those fifteen back with runway, and fifteen more on top. Fisk held his own glove up and squinted at it like it might tell him something. So the tailwind's a loan. At a lousy rate. On a jet this heavy you want every foot.

Right. Log it. A wing doesn't read the ground. I flew with an aircraft commander out of Tolliver who called the windsock the cheapest engine on the field, and he'd turn a runway around for five knots. Point the nose into the wind and part of your airspeed is already there before the brakes come off, so you lift off with runway to spare. Wind at your back, you pay for it in concrete.

At 6:10 Fisk came up on the radio. Wheel's on, Sergeant. Forms are done. Kemp had pulled his airman off at six for his own jet, so Fisk had finished alone. Kit was across the jet with her head in the oil panel, and she said she'd be over.

She read the forms on the hood of her truck first. Wheel removed, wheel installed, and the torque line signed done at 6:05, with his initials next to it. Then she walked to the tool crib for the big torque wrench. Boyd had raised her to check the torque on anything with wheels, everybody's, her own included, and she'd never found a reason to stop.

The big wrench was on its hook behind the crib window, in its case, with the calibration tag still wired to the handle. The airman on the window turned the log around for her without being asked. The last line for that wrench was Thursday afternoon.

It was the only wrench in the crib that went that high. Nobody had torqued the wheel. A nut run down hard by hand looks a lot like a torqued one, and there was no torque stripe on it either, which you'd only catch if you went looking. That was a wheel carrying its share of three hundred thousand pounds down a runway on somebody's guess. Out past the crib window the crew bus was turning in at the far gate.
The torque line is signed, and the wrench never left its hook. What should Kit do first?
A. Call the expediter and hold two two eight until the wheel's torqued.
B. Raise Fisk on the radio and ask him whether he torqued it.
C. Sign out the wrench and torque the wheel herself before the bus comes.
D. Ask around the ramp, in case anybody had another big wrench out.

She keyed the radio. Expediter, two two eight. Hold my jet. Left main needs torque. A pause on the net. Copy, holding. How long? She said she'd call him. She wrote the wheel up in the forms with a red X, so the jet was grounded on paper as well as on the net. Then she signed the big wrench out under her own name, and the kid on the window wrote the time down without looking up at her.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Integrity and Professionalism, and this is the exception. A false record was headed for a jet. The rule's still talk to the person first. The jet just doesn't sit around waiting on that talk. You stopped it at your own level with one call, and you said what was wrong without saying who. The who comes next. Which would you rather explain to a crew, a late jet or a wheel?
The crew truck was idling by the fence. Fisk had his head on the passenger window, out cold sitting up, lanyard and all. In the back, Kemp's two airmen had their hoods up. Neither one was asleep.

Then Boyd's voice on the radio. Darrow. Expediter says your jet's on hold. She told him she'd come to him in fifteen minutes. He said copy and nothing else, which from Boyd meant he'd be standing at his truck in fourteen.
Fisk is in the truck with two of Kemp's airmen. How should Kit start?
A. Open the truck door and ask him there why his initials are on it.
B. Torque it herself, let him sleep for now, and talk to him later.
C. Wait for Boyd to get there, and let Boyd do the asking.
D. Get him out of the truck and walk him to the far side of the jet.

Fisk. Bring my light. He got out fast. She walked him around the nose to the far side, under the left wing by the new wheel, where nobody in the truck could see them. The big wrench never left the crib. He didn't try to talk his way out of it, and later that was the part she kept. He just nodded at the wheel, once. Then they torqued it together, Fisk reading her each step out of the tech data while she leaned on the handle, and after that she did her inspection with him standing there. Nobody signed a thing on that wheel until it was true.

That'll hold, Sergeant. Integrity, with Mentoring in it. The jet was already held, so the hurry had gone out of the morning. That bought him a few minutes away from the truck to tell it himself. He still had to tell Boyd. He just didn't have to tell an audience first. Once the jet's stopped, who should hear it first?
Boyd's truck was at the end of the row with the engine running and the window down. Nobody else on the ramp was paying any attention to two two eight yet.

Fisk was by the new wheel on the cold side of the jet with his hands in his pockets, and he got to it before she could. I said the forms were done. On the radio, at ten after. I knew the big wrench was still on its hook when I keyed the mike.

He'd signed the line so he wouldn't forget it, he said, and meant to go get the wrench, and sat down in the truck to warm his hands first. She asked him why he hadn't just told her at four that he was done in. He kicked the chock, not hard. You'd have pulled me off. And then you'd know.
She had nothing to say to that. Then he took his hands out of his pockets and asked her straight out, the way she'd taught him to ask everything. What are you going to tell him?
A. Walk Fisk to Boyd's truck now and let him tell it with her there.
B. Tell Boyd the wheel needed a recheck, and fix the entry herself.
C. Take the forms past Boyd to the quality office in the hangar.
D. Wave Boyd up to the jet and tell him there, by the crew bus.

Nothing. You're going to tell him, and I'll be standing right there. They walked down the row together. Fisk told it standing up straight, without dressing any of it, the six o'clock and the initials and the radio call, and Kit kept quiet till he was done. Boyd listened with his arm on the window. Then he looked at her. Jet good? Torqued and inspected. Boyd got out, took the forms binder, and corrected the entry himself, the slow way the rules wanted, which took longer than the torque had. Then he turned to Fisk. Go home and sleep. Be here at six tomorrow. You're off torque tasks till Sergeant Darrow retrains you, and this goes up the line in writing. That part isn't mine to skip. Fisk said yes, Master Sergeant, and went. At 8:55 two two eight rolled, twenty five minutes late, and Kit saluted it out.

Right. Log it. Integrity and Professionalism, every piece in order. The jet stopped first. Fisk heard it from you first, in private. And Boyd heard it this morning, from the airman who did it, with you standing next to him. Not Monday, and not secondhand. On the test, covering for somebody lands low, and so does jumping past your supervisor. Once the jet was held, the hurry was over. The report still had to happen today.

Boyd stayed put. He sat there until two two eight was off the ground and turning out over the river, then reached across and shoved the passenger door open. Get in. It's cold. She got in. His heater still smelled like somebody had left a sock on it in 2016.
For a while he just watched the runway. Then, without looking at her, he said it. You put Fisk on that wheel. He came in off ten hours at the warehouse.
There was no anger in it. He said it like a thing he'd already decided, and was waiting on her to decide too.
Boyd isn't asking about Fisk anymore. What should Kit say?
A. Tell him Kemp pulled his airman at six and left Fisk alone.
B. Tell him Fisk said he was good, and she took his word for it.
C. Tell him yes, she saw it at four and let it go.
D. Tell him it's handled now, and she'd rather leave it there.
I saw it at four, Sergeant, and again at the wheel. I let it go. Boyd nodded at the windshield. Neither of them said anything for a good minute.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Integrity, the kind with no audience. He wasn't asking what happened. He was asking whether you'd own your share, and you did, in two short sentences, with no reason in front of them. The officer who owns the problem beats the one who explains it. Where do you suppose he learned to ask it that way?
Then Boyd said it to the windshield. You said yours before I had to ask for it. He put the truck in gear and sat there with his foot on the brake. That's how I'd want the shop run when I'm gone.
Her hand went to her chest pocket, to the work card from January with five weeks on the back of it. There was nothing she could say in that truck that wouldn't have been a lie to him or to herself.
At ten, with the jet out on the track and nothing to do but wait for it, she sat in the crew truck and finally took Vern's log out of her coat.

My log, twenty April, oh one. Tolliver to the track and home, six point one hours. Four receivers at the brief, fourteen thousand pounds each. Offload available, fifty thousand. The plan said four. My miss. Caught it at engine start. Told the aircraft commander before we taxied, and called the receivers' units. Gave number four what was left. Thirty minutes late. The aircraft commander said better here than on the track. I wrote it down so I'd remember whose it was.

She read it twice. In eight weeks of logs it was the first time she'd seen him get anything wrong, and he'd written it in ink, MY MISS, in the same capitals as everything else. He'd picked it on Tuesday for the arithmetic. He couldn't have known.

Hers was folded small under the foam in her toolbox, a score sheet a machine had printed in 2019. She'd never written a word on it. She'd told people whose it was instead, and every time she'd said Boyd.
How far short was the plan Vern briefed?
A. Nothing at all; fifty thousand covers all four of them.
B. Six thousand pounds, fifty six thousand against fifty.
C. Eight thousand pounds, what's left after three full loads.
D. Fourteen thousand pounds, one receiver's whole share.
Four times fourteen thousand is fifty six thousand. Fifty available. Six thousand short. She wrote it in the margin under MY MISS, small, in pencil, and sat looking at his ink for a while.

That'll hold, Sergeant. Multiply what was promised, then subtract what was there. Fifty six thousand less fifty thousand is six thousand. Eight thousand is what's left after three full loads, a different question with a real number in it. Which one did the question ask?

At two that afternoon, with the jet still on the track, she walked across the street to the base test office. The test control officer was a civilian with reading glasses on a chain and a drawer full of vouchers. It took ten minutes, a form and her ID, and she walked out with a voucher number printed on a slip of paper.

She'd sat the test in that building in October 2019, in the room at the end of the hall, and the clock in the hall was the same one. The test control officer tore the slip off, pushed it across, and mentioned that the office gave the computer version now too, end of the hall, any drill Saturday. Kit said Kansas City was fine. She folded the slip into her pocket with the work card and didn't look down the hall.

Graham was at the stove when she got home at six, with a pot of soup going and a stack of lab reports at his elbow. He looked at her face before he looked at anything else, and he turned the burner down before he asked. How was drill? It was the same thing he'd asked in January, at the same counter, and in January she'd answered with the want.
A. Tell him about Fisk, and leave out who put Fisk on the wheel.
B. Tell him it was the kind of day that looks good to a colonel.
C. Say it was long and the jet went late, and ask about his week.
D. Tell him the whole day, her own part in it included.

Fisk signed a torque he didn't do. I caught it. Then she told him the rest, the crib and the hook and the truck and Boyd's window, and then the part she hadn't planned on telling: that she'd looked at Fisk at four in the morning and seen nine and a half hours on him and given him the wheel anyway. Graham stirred the soup. Why didn't he just tell you he was wiped? He said I'd have pulled him. And then I'd know. Graham wanted to know what she'd know. It took her a while. That he couldn't. She heard it come out of her own mouth and stood there at the counter with it. Graham waited, and after a while he got down two bowls.

Right. Log it. Communication. He asked how drill was, and you told him what happened, your part included, without making yourself the hero of it. That's a straight report to the person it's owed to. The test wants the same at work: the whole picture, to the person who needs it, before they have to dig.

At ten that night she sat at the kitchen table with the laptop and the voucher slip, and booked it herself. Graham had gone to bed. He'd picked the date in February, and she'd let him, and tonight she wanted her own hands on it. It was the same chair she'd hit Cancel from in February. She didn't look for Cancel.

The scheduler gave her three Kansas City centers and three Saturdays in a grid, with the first open start time in each cell. Graham had said the north one, in the strip mall off the interstate. It was the closest to the river road.

Three centers down the side, three Saturdays across the top. The north center: May eighth, twelve thirty. May fifteenth, eight o'clock. May twenty second, nine o'clock. The south center: May eighth, eight o'clock. May fifteenth, twelve thirty. May twenty second, eight o'clock. The east center: May eighth, nine o'clock. May fifteenth, nine o'clock. May twenty second, none open.
What does the scheduler show for the north center on May 15?
A. Read 9:00, the last column of the top row.
B. Read 12:30, the first column of the top row.
C. Read 8:00, the middle column of the top row.
D. Read 12:30, second row, middle column.

Finger on the north row, finger on May 15. Eight o'clock. She checked next door both ways, 12:30 to the left and 9:00 to the right, and 12:30 below it in the south row, and clicked the eight. It took eleven minutes in all, most of it finding her ID number.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Row first, then column, then the neighbors, so you know what a slip would have looked like. Eight, with 12:30 and 9:00 on either side and 12:30 below. On the test, many of the wrong answers come from those cells.
An email from Pearson VUE. Subject: Appointment confirmation. Exam: Air Force Officer Qualifying Test. Date: Saturday, May 15, 2027. Time: 8:00 AM. Location: test center, Kansas City, Missouri
On the way to bed she stopped at the fridge. MAY 15 was still in the corner of Graham's board, with its question mark. She licked her thumb and wiped the question mark off, and left the rest.
She was on the river road at 5:30. At 7:10 her phone buzzed in the shop.
A text from Graham. Question mark's gone. I'll drive.

Boyd ran Sunday roll call from the front of the shop. Before it started he caught her at the coffee. You give the safety brief. Yesterday. Your call how. Fisk was in the second row, rested for the first time in months by the look of him, looking at his boots.
Boyd gave her the brief, and Fisk is in the second row. How should Kit give it?
A. Tell the whole story the way it happened, Fisk's name and all.
B. Hand the brief back to Boyd as his to give.
C. Make it about saying you're too tired and leave Fisk's name out.
D. Read the rule on signing for work out loud, and stop there.

She stood up front with her hands in her coat pockets. Yesterday my jet went twenty five minutes late on a wheel torque. Nobody got hurt. I put an airman on that wheel who came in off a night shift. It was all over him at four, and I gave him the wheel anyway. So here's how my crew runs now. If you're too tired to turn the wrench, you're too tired to sign for it, and you tell me. Nobody gets in trouble for telling me. That was the whole brief. At the back Boyd had his arms folded and didn't unfold them, which was how he listened to things he agreed with. In the second row Fisk looked up from his boots.

That'll hold, Sergeant. Leadership and Communication. You told it as your own miss, which it was, and you kept his name out of it. He'd already answered for it to the people who had to hear it. Then you fixed what caused it. Nobody in your crew had a way to say I'm done in without paying for it. The test likes a leader who fixes the cause out loud and handles the person in private.
At noon Fisk sat down on the step of her toolbox cart with a gas station sandwich. Half of it was gone before he said a word.

I've been thinking. I could quit the warehouse. Then I'm not tired, and that's the whole problem fixed. He said it like he'd made up his mind, and like he was hoping somebody would tell him he hadn't.
Fisk says he could quit the warehouse. What should Kit say?
A. Tell him to ask the warehouse for Friday nights off before drill.
B. Ask what the overnights pay for, and plan drill Fridays with him.
C. Tell him that's his business, as long as he shows up rested.
D. Tell him the Guard comes first, and to give the warehouse notice.

What do the overnights pay for? He told her. His truck, and half his mother's rent since last spring. Quitting was the big answer, and he was twenty, and it was the only one he'd come up with. They worked it on the back of a work card. Drill was one weekend a month, so it was one Friday overnight a month, not the whole job. He decided he'd ask his lead for drill Fridays off, and what he'd say, and what he'd do if the answer was no. When he got up he stopped and looked at the jet, at the new wheel and the stencil under the window. Am I still on her? You're still on her. He went back to the wheel well with the rest of his sandwich.

Right. Log it. Mentoring. You asked the question that let him see how big the problem really was, one night a month, and then he fixed it himself. The test favors helping someone solve their own problem over solving it for them. Who's going to ask his lead on Monday, you or him?

Vern kept the heritage room on Saturdays, and on drill weekends he kept it Sundays too, when there were people on base to wander in. Nobody ever wandered in. Kit came at four, when the shop let go, with a pencil.

It was one long room in the old operations building: glass cases, a propeller blade on the wall, an attitude indicator off some long gone jet under glass, and the computer in the corner where he'd read the long rule. Vern had a table cleared and a stack of pages squared on it in his block capitals. His egg timer from home was sitting by the stack, the cracked one he'd glued.
Every block till now has been one subtest at my table. This is the order they'll run it in. Verbal Analogies first. Eight minutes.

Before he'd turned the timer she had the order down the left margin of the first page, a subtest to a line with the minutes beside each one. She did it without thinking. Vern watched her do it. Then he turned the dial.
Item thirteen at four minutes, the way he'd taught her, and she was a little ahead. Item twenty two was the kind she liked. STANZA is to POEM as MOVEMENT is to blank.
A. Write COMPOSER in the blank.
B. Write TEMPO in the blank.
C. Write PROTEST in the blank.
D. Write SYMPHONY in the blank.
A stanza is a section of a poem. A movement is a section of a symphony. She wrote it with forty seconds left and three items to go.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Part to whole. Movement here is the music word, one section of a long piece. Protest is the marching meaning, and tempo is something a movement has, not something it's part of. Did the first pair tell you which meaning to use?
With ten seconds left she put C on the last three, all of them, never slowed down, and the pencil was on the table before the timer rang.
Vern clicked the timer off and pulled the pages over. He left the answers alone. He went to the left margin of page one, the column she'd put down before he ever turned the dial.
Verbal Analogies, eight. Arithmetic Reasoning, twenty nine. Word Knowledge, five. Math Knowledge, twenty two. Reading Comprehension, thirty eight. Situational Judgment, thirty five.
He put his finger on the fifth line. Reading's twenty four. You wrote thirty eight.
Thirty eight was the old paper number, from back before the test went on computers. Vern had never once said it at his table. She'd written it down anyway.

Kit kept quiet. Vern ran his eyes down the answer column to the bottom, C, C, C. Then he looked at her hands. Both of them were flat on the table with the pencil between, the way some man reading rules off a card had told a whole room to do it in 2019. Then he looked at her about as long as it takes to read one line to the period.
He didn't wait for her yes. Egg timer to twenty nine, arithmetic pages over to her side of the table, and he sat back.
